PAGE 1

5.3 Solution Curves / Phase Portraits

Summary of \(\vec{x}' = A\vec{x}\)

Case: \(\lambda\)'s Real and Distinct (\(\lambda < 0\))

Linear System:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & \sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{2} & -2 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors:

\[ \lambda = -1, -4 \] \[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt{2} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \longleftarrow \text{straight line solutions} \]

Straight Line Solutions: Along each eigenvector direction \(\vec{v}\), trajectories remain on the straight line through the origin, described by \(\vec{x}(t) = c e^{\lambda t} \vec{v}\). Since both eigenvalues are negative, trajectories on these lines head directly into the origin as \(t \to \infty\).

Asymptotic Behavior & Classification

  • Origin Behavior: \(t = \infty\) (since \(e^{\lambda t} \to 0\) as \(t \to \infty\) if \(\lambda < 0\)).
  • At \(t \to \infty\), \(e^{-t} > e^{-4t}\) (the \(e^{-4t}\) term decays to zero much faster than \(e^{-t}\)).
  • So near the origin, solution curves become tangent to and follow the eigenvector of \(\lambda = -1\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}\).

Equilibrium Type: Improper Nodal Sink

  • Sink: All solutions go into the origin as \(t \to \infty\).
  • Improper Node: All non-eigenvector trajectories enter the origin tangent to a single straight-line asymptote (the dominant slow eigenvector \(\lambda = -1\)).
PAGE 2

Case: \(\lambda\)'s Real and Distinct (\(\lambda > 0\))

Linear System:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors:

\[ \lambda = 2, 4 \] \[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Concept Note: When both eigenvalues are positive (\(\lambda_1 = 2, \lambda_2 = 4\)), trajectories flow outward away from the origin as \(t \to \infty\), making the origin an unstable source.

Asymptotic Behavior & Classification

  • Origin Behavior: Corresponds to \(t = -\infty\).
  • As \(t \to -\infty\) (near the origin), \(e^{2t} > e^{4t}\) (since \(e^{4t}\) vanishes much faster as \(t \to -\infty\)).
  • Therefore, trajectories leave along \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\) (the eigenvector corresponding to \(\lambda = 2\)) near the origin.

Equilibrium Type: Improper Nodal Source

The origin is an improper nodal source. Solutions emerge from the origin tangent to the slower-growing eigenvector direction \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and bend toward the faster-growing direction \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\) as \(t \to \infty\).

PAGE 3

\(\lambda\)'s Real and Opposite in Signs

Phase Portrait Diagram

Phase Portrait Analysis:

Trajectories approach the origin along the stable manifold (eigenvector \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\) with \(\lambda = -1\)) and diverge along the unstable manifold (eigenvector \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\) with \(\lambda = 3\)).

Linear System:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues: \[ \lambda = 3, \; -1 \]

Eigenvectors: \[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \]

Origin is a saddle point

PAGE 4

\(\lambda\)'s Are Repeated

System Matrix:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues: \[ \lambda = 1, \; 1 \]

Eigenvectors: \[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

(matrix is complete) → not defective

Star Node Phase Portrait

Eigenvalues are equal, so neither eigenvector is more important \(\rightarrow\) solutions are linear combos of both.

Origin is sometimes called a “star node” and is a proper nodal source.

↷ no preferred asymptote

Key Concept:

Because the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity (2 independent eigenvectors for \(\lambda = 1\)), the system scales isotropically, resulting in purely straight-line radial paths away from the origin in all directions.

PAGE 5

Repeated Eigenvalues: Defective Case

System Equations and Eigenvalues

Linear System

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -4 \\ 4 & -7 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigensystem & Multiplicity

\[ \lambda = -3, -3 \quad \implies \quad \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Defect of one (algebraic multiplicity 2, geometric multiplicity 1)

Defective Eigenvalue: Because the matrix has a repeated eigenvalue \(\lambda = -3\) with only one linearly independent eigenvector \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\), the eigenspace is one-dimensional (a defect of 1), meaning there is only one straight-line solution in the phase plane.

Phase Portrait

Classification & Behavior

  • One straight line solution visible along the eigenvector direction \(\vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
  • Trajectories approach the origin tangent to the single eigenvector axis as \(t \to \infty\).

Origin is an improper nodal sink (degenerate node).

PAGE 6

Complex Eigenvalues: Purely Imaginary Case

System and Purely Imaginary Eigenvalues

Linear System

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

\[ \lambda = i, -i, \quad \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2+i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 2-i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

\(\lambda\)'s are purely imaginary (zero real part), so solution curves are ovals (ellipses).

Determining Ellipse Orientation & Tilt

Which orientation does the major axis take?

To find the orientation, decompose the complex eigenvector \(\vec{v}\):

\[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2+i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + i \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

Sum of real and imaginary parts: \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\) gives the direction of the major axis.

* Incomplete — see next page for full derivation

Purely Imaginary Eigenvalues: When \(\operatorname{Re}(\lambda) = 0\), trajectories neither spiral inward nor outward; they form closed periodic orbits (ellipses). The origin is classified as a neutrally stable center.

Phase Portrait & Direction Test

Trajectory Direction Test

Pick test point on positive \(x_1\)-axis: \(\vec{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\)

Evaluate derivative vector:

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad (\text{pointing right, up}) \]

Confirms counter-clockwise circulation.

Equilibrium Classification

Origin is a center

PAGE 7

Ellipse Orientation

Eigenvectors:

\[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + i \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - i \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

form a parallelogram with \( \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \pm \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \)

Geometric Interpretation: The real and imaginary components of a complex eigenvector \( \vec{v} = \vec{u} \pm i\vec{w} \) span the bounding parallelogram in the phase plane. The trajectory is an ellipse inscribed within this parallelogram tangent to its sides at the vector endpoints.

ellipse is inside the parallelogram

PAGE 8

Complex Eigenvalues with Non-Zero Real Part

if real part of \( \lambda \) is not zero, then the ovals grow or shrink as they go around

Linear System

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \]

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

\[ \lambda = -1 + i, \; -1 - i \] \[ \vec{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2+i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}, \; \begin{bmatrix} 2-i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \]

figure out orientation and direction as before

here, real part of \( \lambda \) is negative, so “oval” shrinks as they go

Stability Analysis: The general solution contains a decay term \( e^{\text{Re}(\lambda)t} = e^{-t} \). Since \( \text{Re}(\lambda) = -1 < 0 \), trajectories spiral inward toward the origin as \( t \to \infty \), classifying the fixed point at the origin as an asymptotically stable spiral sink.

origin is a spiral sink

PAGE 9

An unusual case: one eigenvalue is zero

\[ \vec{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \vec{x} \qquad \begin{aligned} \lambda &= 0,\, 5 \\[4pt] \vec{v} &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix},\, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned} \]

gen. solution:

\[ \vec{x} = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 e^{5t} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \]

Along the line spanned by \( \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \) (\( \lambda = 0 \)):

  • Every point on this line is an equilibrium (\( \vec{x}' = \vec{0} \)).
  • No directions / no motion along the line.

Along trajectories parallel to \( \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \) (\( \lambda = 5 \)):

  • Since \( \lambda = 5 > 0 \), solutions move away from the equilibrium line in the direction of the eigenvector.
Conceptual Summary: When \( \det(A) = 0 \), zero is an eigenvalue (\( \lambda = 0 \)). The kernel/null space of \( A \) forms an entire continuous line of equilibria instead of a single isolated critical point at the origin. Because \( e^{0\cdot t} = 1 \), any initial state on this line remains stationary forever. Trajectories starting off the line flow directly outward along lines parallel to the eigenvector of \( \lambda = 5 \).
